name: Vessel Impurity — General Laws (Keilim)
notes: Comprehensive laws of vessel susceptibility to impurity: what makes a vessel susceptible, minimum sizes, when vessels become pure upon breakage, and the distinction between flat and receptacle vessels across all materials

name: Hierarchy of Impurity Grades (Hishtalshelut haTumot)
notes: The graduated levels of impurity transmission — rishon, sheni, shlishi, revi'i — and which sources are av hatumah vs. derivative, as discussed extensively in Keilim ch. 1

name: Grades of Holiness (Dargot Kedushah)
notes: Ten grades of holiness from Land of Israel through the Holy of Holies, and corresponding restrictions on entry for various classes of impure persons, as enumerated in Keilim 1:6-9

name: Earthenware Vessels (Kelei Cheres)
notes: Specific laws unique to earthenware vessels: impurity only through airspace, not through back/outside, completion of manufacture in the kiln, minimum sizes for broken fragments

name: Wooden Vessels (Kelei Etz)
notes: Laws of wooden vessel susceptibility to impurity: flat wooden objects are pure, receptacles are susceptible; minimum sizes; when manufacture is complete; large vessels holding 40 se'ah are pure

name: Metal Vessels (Kelei Matachot)
notes: Laws of metal vessel impurity: susceptibility whether flat or receptacle, reversion to impurity if reforged, vessels attached to the ground are pure, named vessels vs. unnamed, specific rules for swords, needles, keys, wagons

name: Leather Vessels (Kelei Or)
notes: Laws of leather vessels susceptibility to impurity including minimum sizes, when manufacture is complete, susceptibility of hides by intention, midras impurity of various leather goods

name: Glass Vessels (Kelei Zechuchit)
notes: Unique rabbinic extension of impurity laws to glass vessels: flat glass is pure, receptacles are susceptible; breakage purifies; remanufacturing restores susceptibility; tractate Keilim ends with glass vessels

name: Impurity of Ovens and Stoves (Tum'at Tanur veKirayim)
notes: Detailed laws of impurity of ovens, double stoves, and single stoves: when manufacture is complete, minimum sizes, how breakage purifies, the oven of Akhnai, protection of objects inside from impurity transmission

name: Midras Impurity (Tum'at Midras)
notes: Impurity contracted by objects used for lying/sitting/riding by a zav or zavah — its distinct rules from corpse impurity, which vessels are susceptible, minimum sizes for beds and seats

name: Tightly Fitting Cover Protection (Tzamid Patil)
notes: Details of what materials constitute a valid tightly fitting cover, which vessel materials can protect their contents in a tent of a corpse, and minimum hole sizes that invalidate the cover — Keilim chapters 9-10

name: Remnants of Broken Vessels (Gistera / Shiyarei Kelim)
notes: Laws concerning fragments of broken vessels — minimum sizes for continued susceptibility, the principle that remnants do not have remnants, when a repaired vessel reverts to its original status

name: Connected Parts of Vessels (Chibbur Kelim)
notes: When parts of a vessel are considered connected for purposes of impurity transmission — handles, plugs, coverings, ropes, staffs, plumb-lines, and other attachments; measured lengths for various implements (chapters 13, 29)

name: Inner and Outer Sides of Vessels (Penei uGevei Kelim)
notes: Distinction between inner side (susceptible by airspace) and outer side (susceptible only by contact) of vessels; when inner impurity spreads to outer and vice versa; the 'holding place' of vessels (chapter 25)

name: Completion of Manufacture of Vessels (Gemar Melacha)
notes: The principle that vessels only become susceptible to impurity upon completion of their manufacture — what constitutes completion for different vessel types (ovens, beds, baskets, leather goods, cloth)

name: Intention to Make Vessel Susceptible (Kavvanah l'Hachshir Kelim)
notes: The role of intention (as opposed to act) in rendering a vessel susceptible to impurity, and the converse — when intention can render a vessel insusceptible. Vessels become susceptible by intention but cannot be rendered insusceptible except by a change-effecting act (chapter 25-26)

name: Minimum Sizes in Laws of Vessels (Shiurei Kelim)
notes: The extensive system of minimum measurements governing vessel impurity — hole sizes that purify, minimum capacities for susceptibility, standard measures used (olive, fig, pomegranate, egg, log, se'ah), as systematized in chapter 17

name: Standard Halakhic Measures (Shiurim)
notes: The enumeration and definition of standard halakhic measurements — olive, fig, pomegranate, date, egg, barleycorn, lentil, ox-goad thickness, cubit — and what 'moderate size' means for each (Keilim chapter 17)

name: The Standard Cubit (Amah)
notes: The definition and history of the cubit measurement, the two cubits at Shushan HaBirah, difference between building cubit and vessel cubit, application in Temple context

name: Impurity of Cloth and Garments (Tum'at Begadim)
notes: Laws specific to cloth susceptibility to impurity: minimum size of 3x3 fingerbreadths for corpse impurity, 3x3 handbreadths for midras, how remnants are treated, patches and their connection, poor men's patchwork garments (chapters 27-29)

name: Five Grades of Vessel Susceptibility by Material
notes: The hierarchy of vessel materials and their susceptibility: cloth (5 types), sackcloth (4), leather (3), wood (2), earthenware (1) — as enumerated in Keilim 27:1

name: Riding-Upon vs. Sitting-Upon Impurity (Merkav vs. Moshav)
notes: Distinction between objects used for riding (merkav) and objects used for sitting (moshav) — practical halakhic differences in how impurity is transmitted by contact versus carrying (chapter 23)
